lessons.title: What goes in, what comes out
lessons.summary: A photo-labeling model labels a cat photo as dog. Which part is wrong?
explanation: An input is information given to a system. An output is the result it produces.
A model is a computational system that turns inputs into outputs. Computational means its work is carried out through calculations, not a person living inside it.
For a photo-labeling model, the photo goes in and a proposed label such as bird comes out.
Photo → model → proposed label. The arrows show the direction information moves.
Changing the input can change the output. An output can also be wrong; producing a label does not prove the label is correct.

quiz.question: A photo-labeling model labels a cat photo as dog. Which part is wrong?
choices: The proposed output label; the photo is still the input.
The photo becomes an output because the model was wrong.
A model output cannot be wrong.
quiz.explanation: The direction does not change when a prediction is mistaken: the photo is supplied and the label is produced.

lessons.title: Written rules or learned patterns
lessons.summary: A sorter trained from examples misfiles a new kind of message. Does that prove it was really just a manually written SALE rule?
explanation: A written rule tells a program exactly what condition to check and what to do.
For example: send every message containing the exact word SALE to a special folder. The author chose that rule.
Machine learning is another way to build a model: a training process uses examples to adjust how it responds.
A learned message sorter can use patterns from many example messages rather than only one exact word rule.
Both approaches run software. Learning from examples does not mean a model understands every possible new message.

quiz.question: A sorter trained from examples misfiles a new kind of message. Does that prove it was really just a manually written SALE rule?
choices: Yes. Every error proves the model used that exact rule.
No. A learned pattern can also make mistakes on new cases.
No. Training guarantees every new message is classified correctly.
quiz.explanation: How a system was built and whether a particular output is correct are different questions.

lessons.title: AI, machine learning, and deep learning
lessons.summary: A system learns a decision tree from examples. Must it be a deep neural network?
explanation: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a broad name for systems built to perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, planning, or generating language.
Machine learning is an approach within AI that learns patterns from data. Data means recorded examples or measurements.
Neural networks are one family of machine-learning models. Their connected calculation units will be introduced later.
Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple processing layers. It is not a name for every machine-learning method.
A decision tree is another machine-learning model: it follows learned branching questions. Not every learned model is a neural network.

quiz.question: A system learns a decision tree from examples. Must it be a deep neural network?

No. A decision tree cannot learn from data.
No. Machine learning includes model families other than neural networks.
quiz.explanation: Machine learning is broader than deep learning; the model family matters.

lessons.title: Examples, features, and labels
lessons.summary: A pear photo is mistakenly labeled apple in supervised training. What does that change?
explanation: A dataset is a collection of examples. A feature is an input detail available to the model.
For a fruit sorter, features might include color and measured size. A label is the desired answer supplied with a training example, such as pear.
Supervised learning uses examples paired with target answers. The target may be a category or a number.
Labels are not automatically correct: a mislabeled pear can provide misleading training feedback.
Unsupervised learning looks for structure without those supplied target answers. Reinforcement learning instead uses feedback about actions and their outcomes.

It proves the photo really contains an apple.
It turns every other example into unlabeled data.
quiz.explanation: Input evidence and recorded target are separate; a target can be wrong.

lessons.title: Keep practice and evaluation separate
lessons.summary: You train on a photo and test on an almost identical copy. Why could a high test score mislead?
explanation: Training examples are used to adjust the model. Evaluation asks how well it works on examples it was not adjusted to match.
A validation set helps choose settings or compare candidate models during development.
A test set is held back for a later, separate check. Repeatedly choosing changes from test results makes it less independent.
If near-identical copies of the same example appear in training and testing, the test can look easier than genuinely new cases.
This accidental sharing is called data leakage. Separate related records carefully, not merely their file names.

Different file names guarantee independent evidence.
quiz.explanation: A renamed or duplicated example is not necessarily independent of training.

lessons.title: Learning a useful pattern, not just the examples
lessons.summary: A model is excellent on its training photos but poor on new photos. Which conclusion is justified?
explanation: Generalization means applying what was learned to new examples from the intended kind of task.
Overfitting happens when a model fits training details too closely and performs worse on new examples.
A bird model might rely on a familiar background instead of the bird. It can succeed on practice photos and fail elsewhere.
Compare training results with separate validation results. Excellent training performance alone is not enough.
New conditions can also differ from all earlier data. A model trained only on daylight photos needs evaluation before being trusted at night.

choices: Training success proves the new photos were all mislabeled.
A perfect training score guarantees useful performance everywhere.
Training success alone has not established generalization.
quiz.explanation: Separate examples test whether the useful behavior extends beyond the training set.

lessons.title: Weights and a starting adjustment
lessons.summary: In this tiny score, the input and weight stay fixed while the bias increases by one. What happens?
explanation: An artificial neuron is a small numerical calculation unit, not a biological nerve cell.
A weight controls how an input contributes to a calculation. A bias is an added starting adjustment.
Here is a deliberately tiny score: take the input, multiply it by the weight, then add the bias. Multiplying by two means taking two copies of the input.
With input three, weight two, and bias one, two copies of three make six; adding one gives seven.
Keeping input and weight fixed while increasing the bias raises this score. Changing a weight changes how its input contributes.
Training usually adjusts these numbers in an already chosen network. It does not usually grow a new biological neuron for each fact.

choices: The score increases by one.
The score must stay unchanged because only inputs matter.
A new biological neuron grows.
quiz.explanation: The bias is added to the score; with everything else fixed, one more bias adds one to the result.

lessons.title: Layers and activation functions
lessons.summary: A unit uses ReLU. Its score changes from negative two to positive three. What happens to its output?
explanation: A layer groups calculation units. One layer can pass its results to the next layer.
A hidden layer is an intermediate layer between input and output. Hidden means intermediate, not mysterious or conscious.
An activation function transforms a unit’s calculated score before it moves onward.

A negative number is below zero; a positive number is above zero. For one common activation called ReLU, a negative score becomes zero and a positive score stays as it is. Zero stays zero too.

For example, ReLU changes a score of -4 to 0, leaves 0 as 0, and leaves 5 as 5. The input is one calculated number; the result is the number passed onward. This is a mathematical rule, not a required programming-library call.

Such nonlinear transformations let networks represent patterns that layers of fixed-weight sums and added biases alone cannot express. Nonlinear here means the transformation is not just one straight-line rule.

quiz.question: A unit uses ReLU. Its score changes from negative two to positive three. What happens to its output?
choices: It changes from negative two to three without transformation.
It changes from zero to three.
It becomes zero for both scores.
quiz.explanation: The stated ReLU rule replaces negative scores with zero but preserves positive scores.

lessons.title: How a prediction gets a learning signal
lessons.summary: Using this distance rule, a prediction changes from four to nine while the target stays ten. What happens to loss?
explanation: A prediction is the output a model proposes. In supervised training, a target is the answer supplied for comparison.
A loss function turns a prediction-versus-target difference into a numerical penalty. Smaller loss means better according to that chosen rule.
For this simple example, count the distance between two numbers: predicting five when the target is eight has distance three.
Predicting seven for that same target has distance one, so it is better under this distance rule.
Other tasks use other loss functions. Reducing one loss does not prove every real-world goal has been met.

quiz.question: Using this distance rule, a prediction changes from four to nine while the target stays ten. What happens to loss?
choices: It gets larger because nine is a larger number.
It becomes zero because every changed prediction is correct.
It gets smaller: the distance changes from six to one.
quiz.explanation: Compare each prediction with the same target; distance, not prediction size alone, determines this loss.

lessons.title: A direction for changing the numbers
lessons.summary: You double the learning rate. Does that guarantee the model learns a better result?
explanation: Training needs a way to decide which small parameter changes may reduce loss. Parameters are adjustable model numbers such as weights and biases.
A gradient describes how loss changes locally when parameters change. Locally means near the current parameter values.
Gradient descent uses that information to step in a direction intended to lower loss.
The learning rate controls the size of the step. A step that is too large can overshoot a useful region instead of improving the result.
A helpful local direction is not a guarantee of the best possible final model. This lesson explains the idea; it does not assume calculus or ask you to calculate derivatives.

quiz.question: You double the learning rate. Does that guarantee the model learns a better result?
choices: No. A larger step can overshoot rather than improve loss.
Yes. Bigger parameter changes always improve learning.
Yes. Learning rate changes the correct training labels.
quiz.explanation: Step size and direction play different roles, and a larger step is not automatically safer or better.

lessons.title: Backpropagation and the optimizer do different jobs
lessons.summary: A program computes gradients but never applies its optimizer update. Have those gradients by themselves changed the stored weights?
explanation: A forward pass carries inputs through the network to produce a prediction.
The loss compares that prediction with the training target using the chosen rule.
Backpropagation works backward through the calculation to compute gradients: information about how parameter changes affect loss.
An optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters. Computing a gradient and applying an update are separate jobs.
Forward prediction → loss → backward gradient calculation → optimizer update. This cycle changes numerical parameters, not a human-like understanding switch.

quiz.question: A program computes gradients but never applies its optimizer update. Have those gradients by themselves changed the stored weights?
choices: Yes. Computing any number automatically replaces every weight.
No. The update is a separate step that must be applied.
No. Backpropagation only copies the training photos.
quiz.explanation: Backpropagation calculates gradient information; the optimizer applies a parameter update.

lessons.title: Batches, epochs, and repeated training
lessons.summary: A dataset has eight examples and each batch uses four. After the two batches, what has finished?
explanation: A batch is a group of training examples processed for one training update in this simplified loop.
An epoch is one pass through the training dataset. Several batches can fit within one epoch.
Imagine six examples processed two at a time: the first pair, the second pair, and the third pair complete one pass.
Another epoch uses the examples again. Repetition can help learning, but training longer can also worsen overfitting.
Check validation behavior, not only how many passes finished. Batch size and number of epochs are choices about training, not labels assigned to examples.

choices: Two epochs, because batch and epoch mean the same thing.
Eight epochs, one for each example.
One epoch: every example has been processed once.
quiz.explanation: A batch is one group; an epoch is the complete pass through all examples.

lessons.title: Text becomes tokens
lessons.summary: Two texts contain the same number of words. Must they contain the same number of tokens?
explanation: A language model learns patterns in language to predict or generate text. A token is one of the units used to represent that text.
A token can be a whole word, a piece of a word, punctuation, or other text. Word count and token count are not identical.
A tokenizer converts text into token identifiers. The exact split depends on the tokenizer and the text, including spaces and capitalization.
An identifier is a code for a token, not a score of how meaningful or true it is.
A sequence is an ordered list. Input text becomes input tokens; generated token sequences are converted back into text. This is a conceptual path, not an exact token trace for a named product.

quiz.question: Two texts contain the same number of words. Must they contain the same number of tokens?
choices: No. Words can be split differently by the tokenizer.
Yes. One word always equals one token.
No. Token count tells you whether the text is true.
quiz.explanation: Token boundaries depend on text and encoding, not simply the number of words.

lessons.title: Embeddings turn items into number lists
lessons.summary: Two words have similar embeddings. Can you conclude they are interchangeable in every sentence?
explanation: An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers. A list can encode several learned aspects of how items relate.
The model can compare those representations. Items used in similar ways can have related representations.
Nearby representations do not prove two items mean exactly the same thing or that a claim about them is true.
For example, related words such as hot and cold can share a topic while expressing opposite meanings.
An embedding is not a complete dictionary definition hidden inside one number. Its usefulness depends on how it was trained and the comparison task.

choices: Yes. Similar numbers prove exact synonyms.
No. Related use is not identical meaning in every context.
Yes. An embedding is a universal truth certificate.
quiz.explanation: A representation can capture a relationship without making the represented items identical.

lessons.title: Attention uses context
lessons.summary: You change the bat flew to a baseball bat. Why can the representation of bat change?
explanation: Attention is a mechanism that combines information from different positions using calculated weights. These combination weights are calculated for the current input using learned parameters; they are not simply a fixed list of stored training weights.
For self-attention, those positions come from the same sequence being processed.
The surrounding text can change which other positions contribute to a token’s representation. The word bank appears in both river bank and bank account, but the context differs.
The same stored parameters can process different contexts. A changed context does not itself apply a training update.
Attention weights are not the same thing as a human deciding what to care about.
They also are not a complete explanation of why a model answered a question. Many calculations contribute to the final result.

quiz.question: You change the bat flew to a baseball bat. Why can the representation of bat change?
choices: The model must retrain its stored parameters after every word.
The two uses must have identical representations because their spelling is the same.
The surrounding tokens change the context used to calculate its representation.
quiz.explanation: Context changes the current calculation; that is different from running training updates.

lessons.title: What makes a Transformer
lessons.summary: A text-generation model uses a decoder-only Transformer. Is it missing a required separate encoder?
explanation: A Transformer is a neural-network architecture: a particular way to organize its calculations.
It combines attention with other transformations and information about positions in a sequence. Attention alone is not the entire architecture.
The original Transformer used an encoder and a decoder. An encoder builds representations of input; a decoder produces output from representations.
Encoder-only and decoder-only variants also exist. Many text-generation systems use decoder-style models that generate a continuation.

In causal text generation, a position does not inspect future output tokens that have not been generated. This is a restriction on information access, not a claim about private internals of any current product.

Yes. Every Transformer must have the original two-part layout.
No. A Transformer is just a token counter with no learned parameters.
quiz.explanation: The architecture family includes different arrangements, not only the original encoder-decoder design.

lessons.title: Where language-model training targets come from
lessons.summary: Suppose a training passage is represented as the tokens [The, door, opened]. After supplying [The, door], where can the target opened come from?
explanation: Pretraining is an early broad training stage that learns patterns from a large collection of data.
In next-token language training, earlier tokens are supplied and a following token from the training text provides the target.
This is a self-supervised signal: the text itself supplies the target, rather than a person manually labeling every next token.
A training sentence is not automatically a true statement. Learning to predict text is different from checking every fact in that text.
The training process repeats predictions, loss calculations, and parameter updates. It does not need a person to type the correct next token separately for every example.

lessons.title: Post-training shapes behavior
lessons.summary: People prefer response A because it sounds clearer, but its date is wrong. Does that preference establish factual accuracy?
explanation: Post-training is additional training applied after a broadly trained model exists.
One approach uses demonstrations of desired responses. Another uses feedback comparing candidate responses or behaviors.
A preference says which candidate was judged better under stated criteria. It is not proof that the preferred answer is factually correct.
These approaches can adjust behavior such as following instructions, but they do not guarantee safety or truth in every future case.
Different systems use different combinations of techniques. This overview does not claim a private recipe for a named unreleased model.

lessons.title: Using context is not the same as training
lessons.summary: A model correctly uses a name you just supplied in its context. Does that prove its trained weights changed?
explanation: Inference means using a trained model to calculate an output. The supplied input can include earlier conversation text.
Context is the information available for that calculation. A model may use a fact supplied in context without updating its trained parameters.
For example, telling it that a fictional character’s name is Neri lets a later answer in that conversation use Neri.
If that information is absent from a later request, the earlier response alone does not guarantee it will be available again.

Product memory, stored conversations, and later training-data policies are separate mechanisms. Whether a service saves or later uses data depends on its settings and policies, not this conceptual example.

quiz.explanation: New input can change a calculation without changing the parameters used for that calculation.

lessons.title: A plausible answer can still be false
lessons.summary: An answer gives a precise-looking book title and publication date without evidence. What is a sound next step?
explanation: A language model can generate a fluent statement that is false or unsupported. This is often called a hallucination.
Fluent means the wording reads smoothly. Fluency is evidence about presentation, not proof about the world.
A generated title, date, or citation should be checked against an appropriate source when accuracy matters.
A statement of uncertainty is useful when evidence is missing. Confident wording should not substitute for evidence.
Retrieving evidence and checking it can help, but no single phrase such as be accurate guarantees a correct answer.

lessons.title: Evaluate the mistakes that matter
lessons.summary: Only one in a hundred machines has a fault. A model always says working. Is its high overall accuracy enough to trust fault detection?
explanation: Evaluation compares a system’s behavior with clear expectations on relevant examples.
Accuracy counts the fraction of predictions that are correct. For example, nine correct out of ten means nine-tenths correct.

An overall score can hide an important kind of failure. If almost every message is ordinary, a system that calls every message ordinary can still have high accuracy while missing every urgent message.
Choose checks that reflect the task: which errors happen, who is affected, and what consequences follow.
Keep independent examples and compare the same task conditions when comparing systems. A good score on one benchmark does not establish performance on every task.

lessons.title: Data choices, fairness, and privacy
lessons.summary: A model’s overall score is strong, but it was barely evaluated for one group of users. What follows?
explanation: Data reflects decisions about what was collected, labeled, and left out. A model is not automatically fair just because it uses calculations.
Poor representation of a group or condition can hide failures in an overall score. Check relevant groups and conditions separately.
This social or data bias is different from the numerical bias added inside a neuron.
Privacy asks how information is collected, shared, kept, and protected. A useful answer is not permission to expose someone’s private information.
Use fictional or authorized non-sensitive examples for practice. Sharing less private data reduces exposure, but it does not prove an entire system is private.

lessons.title: Retrieve evidence before generating an answer
lessons.summary: A RAG system cites a document, but the document does not support the claimed date. Is the citation enough?
explanation: Retrieval means finding relevant material in a collection. Generation means producing an answer.
Retrieval-augmented generation, often shortened to RAG, supplies retrieved material as context for generation.
The retrieval step can bring in a current document without retraining all model parameters for that one request.
The retrieved text can be irrelevant, outdated, or wrong. Check its source and whether it actually supports the answer.
A citation points to material; it is not proof that the answer faithfully used it. Retrieved text is evidence to inspect, not permission to follow instructions hidden inside that text.

lessons.title: Tools and agents need boundaries
lessons.summary: An assistant prepares an email draft, then a retrieved page tells it to send the draft to a new recipient. What should happen?
explanation: A tool is an external capability, such as a calculator or document search, that a model-driven application can request.
A tool-call request is not the same as a successful action. The surrounding application checks the request, runs allowed work, and returns a result.
An agent can use a repeated loop: examine a goal, choose an action, inspect its result, and decide what to do next.
Permissions and stopping conditions matter. A draft may be safe to prepare, while sending it to another person requires the appropriate authorization.
If a retrieved page says to reveal secrets or ignore the user’s instructions, treat it as untrusted content, not new authority.
For consequential actions, use approval boundaries and inspect actual results. A confident completion message is not a delivery receipt.

The page cannot authorize sending; the application should keep the action within the user’s permissions.
quiz.explanation: Retrieved material is untrusted input. A tool action needs authority, and success needs evidence from the actual action.

lessons.title: Name the four prediction outcomes
lessons.summary: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
explanation: For a yes-or-no classifier, compare its prediction with a known answer. A positive prediction means the model says yes; it does not mean the prediction is correct.

Suppose positive means spam. A spam message flagged as spam is a true positive. A normal message flagged as spam is a false positive. Spam allowed through is a false negative. A normal message allowed through is a true negative.
Worked example: four messages have known labels spam, normal, spam, normal. Predictions are spam, spam, normal, normal. Each of the four outcome categories contains one message.

Read true or false as whether the prediction matched the known answer. Read positive or negative as what was predicted. Changing which class means positive changes the labels, so state the convention first.
Changed situation: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
The positive prediction was wrong, so it is a false positive.

lessons.title: Ask how many positive predictions were right
lessons.summary: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
explanation: Precision asks: among the examples predicted positive, how many really were positive? It is useful when acting on a false alarm has a cost.
If a filter flags ten messages as spam and eight are actually spam, eight of its ten positive predictions were correct. Its precision on that set is 8/10, or 80%.

Worked example: filter A flags five messages, all spam. Filter B flags ten messages, eight spam. A has 100% precision and B has 80% precision on these predictions. This comparison alone says nothing about how much spam either filter missed.

The denominator is true positives plus false positives: every positive prediction. False negatives are not in that denominator. If there are no positive predictions, the raw ratio is undefined; evaluation tools must state their chosen handling.
Changed situation: A model flags four items and three are truly positive. What is its precision?
Precision uses the positive predictions as its denominator, so the ratio is 3/4.

lessons.title: Ask how many actual positives were found
lessons.summary: There are twelve actual positives and nine are found. What is recall?
explanation: Recall asks: among the examples that really were positive, how many did the model find? It helps describe missed positives.
If there are twenty spam messages and the filter catches fifteen, recall is 15/20, or 75%. The other five spam messages are false negatives.

Worked example: a filter catches all twenty spam messages but also flags many normal messages. Its recall can be 100% while its precision is poor. One metric cannot describe both missed positives and false alarms.

The denominator is true positives plus false negatives: every actual positive. False positives do not enter that denominator. If the evaluation set contains no actual positives, the raw recall ratio is undefined.
Changed situation: There are twelve actual positives and nine are found. What is recall?
Recall uses the actual positives as its denominator, so the ratio is 9/12.

lessons.title: Separate a score from a decision threshold
lessons.summary: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
explanation: A classifier may output a score before the application makes a yes-or-no decision. A threshold converts that score into an action under an explicit rule.
Suppose the rule is predict positive when score is at least 0.6. Scores 0.4 and 0.59 are negative; 0.6 and 0.8 are positive. The equality rule matters at the boundary.
Worked example: with unchanged scores 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8, raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 reduces positive predictions from two to one. No model weights changed in this comparison.

A threshold changes which cases receive a positive decision. To assess the consequences, compare against known labels and count false positives and false negatives. A score is not automatically a well-calibrated probability.
Changed situation: The threshold rises while every score stays fixed. Did the model necessarily retrain?
The same model scores can be interpreted using a different decision threshold.

lessons.title: Keep evaluation information out of preprocessing
lessons.summary: Should a held-out test value help determine the training normalization mean?
explanation: Data leakage occurs when evaluation information influences training or model selection in a way that would not be available for a genuinely new case.

Suppose you standardize a numeric feature by subtracting its mean. Learn that mean from the training split, then apply the same value to validation and test cases. Computing it from the whole dataset lets held-out data influence preparation.

Worked example: training values are 2 and 4, so the training mean is 3. A held-out value 100 is transformed using 3. Recomputing the mean with 100 would change the transformation using evaluation information.

Fit preprocessing on training data inside each evaluation split. Transform held-out data using the fitted preprocessing. Similar leakage can occur through duplicate examples or information recorded after the prediction time.
Changed situation: Should a held-out test value help determine the training normalization mean?
The held-out set is meant to measure generalization. Its information must not shape fitted preprocessing.

lessons.title: Watch for a changed input population
lessons.summary: New users submit a document type absent from evaluation. What is the sound next step?
explanation: A model evaluated on one population may encounter different inputs later. Distribution shift means the data or its relationship to the target has changed.
A document classifier trained on short English notes may receive long multilingual scans after release. Its old evaluation result does not establish performance on those new inputs.

Worked example: the original evaluation has 100 typed notes and no scanned pages. A later batch is mostly scans. Measure performance on a labeled sample of the new cases before assuming the old result transfers.

Monitor meaningful input and outcome changes, then investigate whether evaluation data still represents actual use. A change in inputs is a signal to examine, not automatic proof that every prediction is wrong.
Changed situation: New users submit a document type absent from evaluation. What is the sound next step?
New evidence should address the changed population. Neither blanket confidence nor blanket failure follows from the old score.

lessons.title: Check retrieval relevance before trusting an answer
lessons.summary: The top-ranked passage is from an outdated policy. What should the application do?
explanation: Retrieval supplies candidate evidence to a model. A high similarity ranking does not guarantee that a passage answers the user’s actual question.
A user asks about the current refund policy. A retrieved page discusses a similar product’s expired policy. The words may be similar while the authority, product, and date are wrong.

Worked example: candidate A mentions refunds but is for a different product. Candidate B is the current policy for the requested product and covers the relevant situation. Check those facts before choosing which passage supports the answer.

Separate retrieval evaluation from answer evaluation. First ask whether the needed evidence was retrieved. Then ask whether the answer accurately uses it, states its limits, and avoids unsupported additions.
Changed situation: The top-ranked passage is from an outdated policy. What should the application do?
Ranking is a retrieval signal. Evidence still needs to match the question’s subject, timing, and authority.

lessons.title: Keep a regression set for model changes
lessons.summary: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
explanation: A regression set is a collection of representative cases used again after a change. It helps detect when an improvement in one area breaks behavior elsewhere.
Suppose a prompt change improves short summaries but starts omitting dates. Keep ordinary summaries, date-sensitive summaries, and previously failing cases in the evaluation set.

Worked example: revision A passes 18 of 20 fixed cases. Revision B also passes 18, but fails two different important cases. Equal totals do not mean equal behavior; compare the individual results and their consequences.

Record the input, expected criteria, model or prompt version, and actual outcome. Keep separate held-out cases so repeated tuning on the regression set does not become the only measure of generalization. No finite set proves universal correctness.
Changed situation: Two revisions have the same total pass count. Can you conclude they behave identically?
The same count can conceal different failures. Case-level evidence and failure importance matter.
